topic: SC: the 24-hour limit to produce an arrested person before a magistrate (Article 22(2)) runs from actual detention, not from when the arrest is formally recorded; no 'buffer' detention before arrest; only travel time excluded; detention must also be reasonable under Section 58 BNSS; magistrates must record actual time of detention and can refuse remand; NDPS Section 37 cannot override Article 21/22 safeguards; accused released (Sujit Das v. Union of India, Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar, 5 Nov 2026)

slides.title: The **24-hour clock** starts when police **hold you**
slides.subtitle: Not when they finally write down the arrest. Police cannot buy extra time on paper.
slides.cite: **Sujit Das v. Union of India** · Supreme Court

slides.label: The case
slides.title: Held first, **arrested later**
bullets: In a drug case, the accused was taken into the search team's control around **2 PM on 29 September 2025**.
The arrest was recorded only on **30 September**, after an **18-hour gap** that the agency never explained.
Production before a magistrate came at **4:45 PM on 30 September**, more than 24 hours after the detention began.

slides.label: What the Court held
slides.title: Detained means **arrested**
bullets: Under **Article 22(2)**, the 24 hours run from the moment a person is **actually detained**, whatever the arrest memo says.
Police cannot keep someone in a **'buffer zone'** of custody before formally arresting them. The Court called this unconstitutional.
Only the **travel time** needed to reach the magistrate's court can be left out of the 24 hours.
slides.note: **Law fact:** Article 22(2) says an arrested person must be produced before the **nearest magistrate within 24 hours**.

slides.label: More safeguards
slides.title: 24 hours is the **outer limit**
bullets: Even within 24 hours, detention must be **reasonable** under **Section 58 BNSS**. An unexplained 18-hour delay was not.
Magistrates must note the **actual date and time of detention** and may **refuse remand** if the hold was unreasonably long.
Strict NDPS bail rules (**Section 37**) cannot override these constitutional rights. The accused was ordered **released**.

slides.label: Keep in mind
slides.title: This is about **liberty**, not guilt
bullets: The release was ordered because the **24-hour limit was broken**. The ruling does not say the accused is innocent.
If police take someone in, note **when and where** it happened. Under this ruling, that is when the 24 hours begin.
This post is for information only, not legal advice.

caption:
Police held you on Monday but 'arrested' you on Tuesday? The Supreme Court says the 24-hour clock started on Monday ⏱️⚖️

In a drug case, the accused came under the search team's control around 2 PM on 29 September 2025. The arrest was recorded only the next day, after an unexplained 18-hour gap, and the accused was produced before a magistrate at 4:45 PM on 30 September. The agency argued the 24 hours began only from the recorded arrest.

The Court disagreed. Under Article 22(2), the 24 hours run from actual detention, not from the arrest memo. Police cannot create a 'buffer zone' of custody before a formal arrest, and only necessary travel time to the court can be excluded. Even within 24 hours, detention must be reasonable under Section 58 BNSS. Magistrates must record the actual time of detention and can refuse remand if the hold was unreasonably long.

The Court also said strict NDPS bail conditions under Section 37 cannot override these constitutional safeguards, and ordered the accused released. Remember: this was about the breach of the 24-hour rule, not a finding of innocence.

Case: Sujit Das v. Union of India (Supreme Court, 5 Nov 2026)
Bench: Justice Ujjal Bhuyan and Justice Atul S Chandurkar
